arXiv:2103.04265v2 [math.AP] 18 Mar 2021

Persistence and convergence in parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system with logistic source on ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}

Wenxian Shen Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Statistics    Shuwen Xue Affiliation: Auburn University, Auburn, AL 36849, U.S.A.
Abstract

In the current paper, we consider the following parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system with logistic source on ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N},

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+u(a−bu),x∈ℝN,t>0vt=Δv−λv+μu,x∈ℝN,t>0.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+u(a-bu),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\,\,\,t>0\\ {v_{t}}=\Delta v-\lambda v+\mu u,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\,\,\,t>0.\end{cases} (0.1)

where χ,a,b,λ,μ\chi,\ a,\ b,\ \lambda,\ \mu are positive constants and NN is a positive integer. We investigate the persistence and convergence in (0.1). To this end, we first prove, under the assumption b>N​χ​μ4b>\frac{N\chi\mu}{4}, the global existence of a unique classical solution (u⁡(x,t,u0,v0),v⁡(x,t,u0,v0))(u(x,t;u_{0},v_{0}),v(x,t;u_{0},v_{0})) of (0.1) with u⁡(x,0,u0,v0)=u0​(x)u(x,0;u_{0},v_{0})=u_{0}(x) and v⁡(x,0,u0,v0)=v0​(x)v(x,0;u_{0},v_{0})=v_{0}(x) for every nonnegative, bounded, and uniformly continuous function u0​(x)u_{0}(x), and every nonnegative, bounded, uniformly continuous, and differentiable function v0​(x)v_{0}(x). Next, under the same assumption b>N​χ​μ4b>\frac{N\chi\mu}{4}, we show that persistence phenomena occurs, that is, any globally defined bounded positive classical solution with strictly positive initial function u0u_{0} is bounded below by a positive constant independent of (u0,v0)(u_{0},v_{0}) when time is large. Finally, we discuss the asymptotic behavior of the global classical solution with strictly positive initial function u0u_{0}. We show that there is K=K⁡(a,λ,N)>N4K=K(a,\lambda,N)>\frac{N}{4} such that if b>K​χ​μb>K\chi\mu and λ≥a2\lambda\geq\frac{a}{2}, then for every strictly positive initial function u0​(⋅)u_{0}(\cdot), it holds that

limt→∞[‖u⁡(x,t,u0,v0)−ab‖∞+‖v⁡(x,t,u0,v0)−μλ​ab‖∞]=0.\lim_{t\to\infty}\big[\|u(x,t;u_{0},v_{0})-\frac{a}{b}\|_{\infty}+\|v(x,t;u_{0},v_{0})-\frac{\mu}{\lambda}\frac{a}{b}\|_{\infty}\big]=0.

Key words. Parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system, logistic source, classical solution, global existence, persistence, asymptotic behavior.

2010 Mathematics Subject Classification. 35A01, 35B35, 35B40, 35Q92, 92C17.

1 Introduction and the Statements of Main results

The current paper is devoted to the study of the asymptotic dynamics of the following parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis model with logistic source on ℝN{\mathbb{R}}^{N}:

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+u(a−bu),x∈ℝN,vt=Δv−λv+μu,x∈ℝN,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+u(a-bu),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\\ {v_{t}}=\Delta v-\lambda v+\mu u,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\end{cases} (1.1)

where u⁡(x,t)u(x,t)and v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) denote the population densities of some mobile species and chemical substance, respectively; χ>0\chi>0 represents the chemotactic sensitivity effect on the mobile species; λ>0\lambda>0 represents the degradation rate of the chemical substance and μ\mu is the rate at which the mobile species produces the chemical substance. The reaction term u⁡(a−b​u)u(a-bu) in the first equation of (1.1) is referred to as logistic source describing the local dynamics of the mobile species.

The origin of chemotaxis models was introduced by Keller and Segel at the beginning of 1970s in their works [11], [12] to describe the aggregation of the slime mold Dyctyostelium discoideum. Chemotaxis describes the oriented movements of biological cells and organisms in response to chemical gradient which they may produce by themselves over time and is crucial for many aspects of behaviour such as the location of food sources, avoidance of predators and attracting mates, slime mold aggregation, tumor angiogenesis, embryo development, primitive streak formation and etc.(see [21]). A lot of literature is concerned with mathematical analysis of various chemotaxis models. The reader is referred to [1, 7, 8] and the references therein for some detailed introduction into the mathematics of chemotaxis models.

Consider chemotaxis models. Central problems include the existence of non-negative classical/weak solutions which are globally defined in time or blow up at a finite time and the asymptotic behavior of globally defined solutions such as persistence and convergence as time goes to infinity; etc. Considerable progress has been made in the analysis of various chemotaxis models towards these central problems on both bounded and unbounded domains. For example, consider the following chemotaxis model on bounded domain with Neumann boundary condition

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+f(u,v),x∈Ω,vt=Δv−v+u,x∈Ω,∂u∂n=∂v∂n=0,x∈∂Ω.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+f(u,v),\quad x\in\Omega,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,\quad x\in\Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial n}=0,\quad x\in\partial\Omega.\end{cases} (1.2)

Chemotaxis model (1.2) is the so-called minimal model when f≡0f\equiv 0. It is known that finite time blow up may occur for the minimal model. For example, when Ω\Omega is a ball in ℝN{\mathbb{R}}^{N} with N≥3N\geq 3, then for all M>0M>0 there exists positive initial data (u0,v0)∈C⁡(Ω¯)×W1,∞​(Ω)(u_{0},v_{0})\in C(\bar{\Omega})\times W^{1,\infty}(\Omega) with ∫Ωu0=M\int_{\Omega}u_{0}=M such that the corresponding solution blows up in finite time (see [35]). When Ω\Omega is a convex bounded domain with smooth boundary, f⁡(u,v)=u⁡(a−b​u)f(u,v)=u(a-bu) where aa and bb are positive constants, and bχ\frac{b}{\chi} is sufficiently large, it is shown in [36] that unique global classical solution of (1.2) exists for every positive initial data (u0,v0)∈C0​(Ω¯)×W1,∞​(Ω)(u_{0},v_{0})\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega})\times W^{1,\infty}(\Omega) and that the constant solution (ab,ab)(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b}) is asymptotically stable in the sense that

limt→∞[‖u⁡(⋅,t,u0,v0)−ab‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t,u0,v0)−ab‖L∞​(Ω)]=0.\lim_{t\to\infty}\big[\|u(\cdot,t;u_{0},v_{0})-\frac{a}{b}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|v(\cdot,t;u_{0},v_{0})-\frac{a}{b}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\big]=0.

However, when bb is not large relative to χ\chi, numerical evidence shows that even in the spatially one-dimensional setting solutions may exhibit chaotic behavior (see [22]). Also a phenomenon suggested by the numerical simulations in [22] consists in the ability of (1.2) to enforce asymptotic smallness of the cell population density, undistinguishable from extinction, in large spatial regions (see e.g. Fig. 7(d) in [22]). In [28], the authors proved that any such extinction phenomenon must be localized in space, and that the population as a whole always persists, which is called persistence of mass in [28]. Recently, Issa and Shen [10] proved the pointwise persistence phenomena, that is, any globally defined positive solution is bounded below by a positive constant independent of its initial data, which implies that the cell population may become very small at some time and some location, but it persists at any location eventually. For other related works on (1.2), we refer the readers to [9, 14, 15, 16, 19, 20, 33] and references therein.

When the second equation of (1.2) is replaced by 0=Δ​v−v+u,x∈Ω0=\Delta v-v+u,\,x\in\Omega, it becomes

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+f(u,v),x∈Ω,0=Δv−v+u,x∈Ω,∂u∂n=∂v∂n=0,x∈∂Ω.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+f(u,v),\quad x\in\Omega,\\ 0=\Delta v-v+u,\quad x\in\Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial n}=0,\quad x\in\partial\Omega.\end{cases} (1.3)

(1.3) is referred to as the parabolic-elliptic chemotaxis model which models the situation in which the chemical substance diffuses very quickly. Global existence, finite blow up and asymptotic behavior of parabolic-elliptic chemotaxis model has also been studied in many papers. For example, when f⁡(u,v)=u⁡(a−b​u)f(u,v)=u(a-bu) where aa and bb are positive constants, it is proved in [29] that unique bounded global classical solution (u⁡(x,t,u0),v⁡(x,t,u0))(u(x,t;u_{0}),v(x,t;u_{0})) with u⁡(x,0,u0)=u0​(x)u(x,0;u_{0})=u_{0}(x) exists for any sufficiently smooth positive initial function u0u_{0}, under the assumption that either N≤2N\leq 2 or b>N−2N​χb>\frac{N-2}{N}\chi, and that in presence of certain sufficiently strong logistic damping, the constant solution (ab,ab)(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b}) is asymptotically stable. For other studies of parabolic-elliptic chemotaxis models on bounded domains, we refer the readers to [3, 5, 13, 30, 31, 34, 37, 38, 40] and the references therein.

There are also several studies of chemotaxis models on the whole space. For example, consider (1.1) when f⁡(u,v)=0f(u,v)=0. It is possible for a non-negative solution in ℝN{\mathbb{R}}^{N} (N≥2N\geq 2) to blow up in finite time (see [2]). It was shown in [17] that the unique solution exists globally in time and bounded under some conditions for initial data. Moreover, every bounded solution decays to 00 as t→∞t\to\infty and behaves like the heat kernel with the self-similarity (see [18] for the asymptotic profiles of bounded solution in the case N=1N=1).

When the second equation in (1.1) being replaced by 0=Δ​v−λ​v+μ​u0=\Delta v-\lambda v+\mu u, it becomes

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+u(a−bu),x∈ℝN,0=Δv−λv+μu,x∈ℝN.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+u(a-bu),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\\ 0=\Delta v-\lambda v+\mu u,\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}.\end{cases} (1.4)

Some studies of (1.4) are also carried out. For example, in the case of a=b=0a=b=0, it is known that blow-up occurs if either N=2 and the total initial population mass is large enough, or N≥3N\geq 3 (see [1], [4] and references therein). When aa and bb are positive constants, it is shown for the case λ=μ=1\lambda=\mu=1 in [24] that if b>χb>\chi, then there exists a unique bounded global classical solution for any nonnegative initial u0∈Cunifb​(ℝN)u_{0}\in C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}), and that if b>2​χb>2\chi, then for any strictly positive initial infx∈ℝNu0​(x)>0\inf_{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}u_{0}(x)>0, the unique global classical solution (u⁡(x,t,u0),v⁡(x,t,u0))(u(x,t;u_{0}),v(x,t;u_{0})) with u⁡(x,0,u0)=u0​(x)u(x,0;u_{0})=u_{0}(x) converges to constant solution (ab,ab)(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b}) as time goes to infinity. For the persistence of globally defined classical solution with strictly positive initial function, we refer the readers to [26]. For the asymptotic behavior of nonempty compact supported initials and front like initials on the whole space ℝN{\mathbb{R}}^{N}, we refer the readers to [25] and [27].

There is not much study of the asymptotic dynamics in (1.1). The objective of the current paper is to investigate the persistence of global classical solution of (1.1) with strictly positive initial data and the asymptotic behavior of global classical solution of (1.1) with strictly positive initial data.

In the rest of this introduction, we introduce the notations and definitions, and state the main results of this paper.

1.1 Notations and statements of the main results

In order to state our main results, we first introduce some notations and definitions. Let

Cunifb​(ℝN)={u∈C⁡(ℝN)|u⁡(x)​is uniformly continuous in​x∈ℝN​and​supx∈ℝN|u⁡(x)|<∞}C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})=\{u\in C({\mathbb{R}}^{N})\,|\,u(x)\,\,\text{is uniformly continuous in}\,\,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\,\,{\rm and}\,\,\sup_{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}|u(x)|<\infty\}

equipped with the norm ‖u‖∞=supx∈ℝN|u⁡(x)|\|u\|_{\infty}=\sup_{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}|u(x)|, and

Cunifb,1={u∈Cunifb(ℝN)|∂xiu∈Cunifb(ℝN),i=1,2,⋯,N}C_{\rm unif}^{b,1}=\{u\in C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})\,|\,\partial_{x_{i}}u\in C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}),\,\,i=1,2,\cdots,N\}

equipped with the norm ‖u‖Cunifb,1=‖u‖∞+∑i=1N‖∂xiu‖∞\|u\|_{C_{\rm unif}^{b,1}}=\|u\|_{\infty}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|\partial_{x_{i}}u\|_{\infty} and

Cunifb,2={u∈Cunifb,1(ℝN)|∂xi​xju∈Cunifb(ℝN),i,j=1,2,⋯,N}.C_{\rm unif}^{b,2}=\{u\in C_{\rm unif}^{b,1}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})\,|\,\partial_{x_{i}x_{j}}u\in C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}),\,\,i,j=1,2,\cdots,N\}.

For given 0<ν<10<\nu<1, let

Cunifb,ν​(ℝN)={u∈Cunifb​(ℝN)|supx,y∈ℝN,x≠y|u⁡(x)−u⁡(y)||x−y|ν<∞}C^{b,\nu}_{\rm unif}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})=\{u\in C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})\,|\,\sup_{x,y\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},x\not=y}\frac{|u(x)-u(y)|}{|x-y|^{\nu}}<\infty\} (1.5)

with the norm ‖u‖∞,ν=supx∈ℝN|u⁡(x)|+supx,y∈ℝN,x≠y|u⁡(x)−u⁡(y)||x−y|ν\|u\|_{\infty,\nu}=\sup_{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}|u(x)|+\sup_{x,y\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},x\not=y}\frac{|u(x)-u(y)|}{|x-y|^{\nu}}. Hence Cunifb,0​(ℝN)=Cunifb​(ℝN)C^{b,0}_{\rm unif}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})=C^{b}_{\rm unif}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}). For 0<θ<10<\theta<1, let

Cθ​((t1,t2),Cunifb,ν​(ℝN))\displaystyle C^{\theta}((t_{1},t_{2}),C_{\rm unif}^{b,\nu}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}))
={u⁡(⋅)∈C⁡((t1,t2),Cunifb,ν​(ℝN))|u⁡(t)​is locally Hölder continuous with exponent​θ}.\displaystyle=\{u(\cdot)\in C((t_{1},t_{2}),C_{\rm unif}^{b,\nu}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}))\,|\,u(t)\,\,\text{is locally H\"{o}lder continuous with exponent}\,\,\theta\}.

We call (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))(u(x,t),v(x,t)) a classical solution of (1.1) on [0,T)[0,T) if u,v∈C⁡(ℝN×[0,T))∩C2,1​(ℝN×(0,T))u,v\in C({\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,T))\cap C^{2,1}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times(0,T)) and satisfies (1.1) for (x,t)∈ℝN×(0,T)(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times(0,T) in the classical sense. A classical solution (u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t))(u(x,t),v(x,t)) of (1.1) on [0,T)[0,T) is called non-negative if u⁡(x,t)≥0u(x,t)\geq 0 and v⁡(x,t)≥0v(x,t)\geq 0 for all (x,t)∈ℝN×[0,T)(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,T). A global classical solution of (1.1) is a classical solution on [0,∞)[0,\infty). Note that, due to biological interpretations, only non-negative classical solutions will be of interest.

The first theorem is on the local existence of a unique classical solution with initial function (u0,v0)∈Cunifb​(ℝN)×Cunifb,1​(ℝN)(u_{0},v_{0})\in C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})\times C_{\rm unif}^{b,1}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}).

Theorem 1.1.

u⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0)∈C⁡([0,Tmax),Cunifb​(ℝN))∩C1​((0,Tmax),Cunifb​(ℝN)),u(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})\in C([0,T_{\max}),C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}))\cap C^{1}((0,T_{\max}),C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})), (1.6)
v⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0)∈C⁡([0,Tmax),Cunifb,1​(ℝN))∩C1​((0,Tmax),Cunifb,1​(ℝN)),v(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})\in C([0,T_{\max}),C_{\rm unif}^{b,1}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}))\cap C^{1}((0,T_{\max}),C_{\rm unif}^{b,1}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})), (1.7)
u⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0),∂xiu⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0),∂xi​xj2u⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0),∂tu⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0)∈Cθ​((0,Tmax),Cunifb,ν​(ℝN))u(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0}),\,\partial_{x_{i}}u(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0}),\,\partial^{2}_{x_{i}x_{j}}u(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0}),\,\partial_{t}u(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})\in C^{\theta}((0,T_{\max}),C^{b,\nu}_{\rm unif}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})) (1.8)
v⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0),∂xiv⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0),∂xi​xj2v⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0),∂tv⁡(⋅,⋅,u0,v0)∈Cθ​((0,Tmax),Cunifb,ν​(ℝN))v(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0}),\,\,\partial_{x_{i}}v(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0}),\,\,\partial^{2}_{x_{i}x_{j}}v(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0}),\,\,\partial_{t}v(\cdot,\cdot;u_{0},v_{0})\in C^{\theta}((0,T_{\max}),C^{b,\nu}_{\rm unif}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})) (1.9)

for all i,j=1,2,⋯,Ni,j=1,2,\cdots,N, 0<θ≪10<\theta\ll 1, and 0<ν≪10<\nu\ll 1. Moreover, if Tmax<∞,T_{\max}<\infty, then limt→Tmax(‖u⁡(⋅,t,u0,v0)‖∞+‖v⁡(⋅,t,u0,v0)‖Cunifb,1​(ℝN))=∞.\lim_{t\to T_{\max}}\big(\left\|u(\cdot,t;u_{0},v_{0})\right\|_{\infty}+\|v(\cdot,t;u_{0},v_{0})\|_{C_{\rm unif}^{b,1}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})}\big)=\infty.

1.2 Remarks on the main results

In this subsection, we provide the following remarks on the main results established in this paper.

  • 1.

    Theorem 1.1 is on the local existence of a unique classical solution with nonnegative initial function (u0,v0)∈Cunifb​(ℝN)×Cunifb,1​(ℝN)(u_{0},v_{0})\in C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})\times C_{\rm unif}^{b,1}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}).     Consider the following general parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis model on bounded domain with Neumann boundary condition

    {ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+f(u,v),x∈Ω,τvt=Δv−v+u,x∈Ω,∂u∂n=∂v∂n=0,x∈∂Ω.\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+f(u,v),\quad x\in\Omega,\\ \tau v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,\quad x\in\Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial n}=0,\quad x\in\partial\Omega.\end{cases} (1.16)

    where τ>0\tau>0 is a positive constant related to the diffusion rate of the chemical substance. Winkler [32] considered the system (1.16) in a smooth bounded convex domain Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{N} with τ>0\tau>0 (τ\tau is not necessarily 1), f⁡(u,v)=u⁡(a−b​u)f(u,v)=u(a-bu) where aa and bb are positive constants, χ∈ℝ\chi\in{\mathbb{R}} and established the global existence and boundedness of non-negative classical solutions of system (1.16) provided that bb is large enough. In [39], Zheng, Li, Bao and Zou extended Winkler’s global existence result to bounded domains (not necessarily convex) of ℝN{\mathbb{R}}^{N} for χ>0\chi>0 and proved that if the logistic dampening b>(N−2)+N​χ​[CN2+1]1N2+1b>\frac{(N-2)_{+}}{N}\chi[C_{\frac{N}{2}+1}]^{\frac{1}{\frac{N}{2}+1}}, where CN2+1C_{\frac{N}{2}+1} is a positive constant which is corresponding to the maximal Sobolev regularity, then (1.16) admits a unique, smooth,and bounded global non-negative solution. Recently, Issa and Shen [10] extended the global existence results obtained in both [32] and [39] to the general full chemotaxis model (1.16) with ff being local as well as nonlocal time and space dependent logistic source. The global existence of classical solutions of (1.16) with τ≠1\tau\not=1 and ff being logistic source on the whole space ℝN{\mathbb{R}}^{N} will be studied somewhere else.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In section 2, we present some preliminary materials that will be needed in the proofs of our main results. In section 3, we study the local and global existence of the classical solution of (1.1) with given initial function and prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. In section 4, we explore the persistence of the global classical solution of (1.1) with strictly positive initial u0u_{0} and prove Theorem 1.3. The last section is devoted to discuss the asymptotic behavior of global classical solutions and prove Theorem 1.4.

3 Local and global existence of classical solutions

This section is devoted to the study of the local and global existence of classical solutions of (1.1) with given initial functions and prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. Throughout this section, unless specified otherwise, CC denotes a generic constant independent of u,vu,v and may be different at different places.

3.1 Proof of Theorem 1.1

In this subsection, we prove Theorem 1.1. The main tools for the proof of this theorem are based on the contraction mapping theorem and the existence of classical solutions for linear parabolic equations with Hölder continuous coefficients. Throughout this subsection, X1=Cunifb​(ℝN)X_{1}=C_{\rm unif}^{b}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}), X2=Cunifb,1​(ℝN)X_{2}=C_{\rm unif}^{b,1}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}), and XiαX_{i}^{\alpha} is the fractional power space of λ​I−Δ\lambda I-\Delta acting on XiX_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2 (α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1)).

(ii) Regularity and non-negativity. We next prove that the mild solution (u⁡(⋅),v⁡(⋅))(u(\cdot),v(\cdot)) of (1.1) on [0,Tmax)[0,T_{\max}) obtained in (i) is a non-negative classical solution of (1.1) on [0,Tmax)[0,T_{\max}) and satisfies (1.6), (1.7), (1.8) and (1.9).

vt=(Δ−λ​I)​v+μ​u​(x,t),x∈ℝN,  0<t<Tmax,v_{t}=(\Delta-\lambda I)v+\mu u(x,t),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\,\,0<t<T_{\max}, (3.7)

are also locally Hölder continuous in t∈(0,Tmax)t\in(0,T_{\max}). Moreover, since u0≥0u_{0}\geq 0 and v0≥0v_{0}\geq 0, by comparison principle for parabolic equations, we get u⁡(x,t,u0,v0)≥0u(x,t;u_{0},v_{0})\geq 0 and v⁡(x,t,u0,v0)≥0v(x,t;u_{0},v_{0})\geq 0 for all x∈ℝx\in{\mathbb{R}}, 0≤t<Tmax0\leq t<T_{\max}.

(iii) Uniqueness. In this section, we investigate the persistence of global classical solutions of (1.1) with strictly positive initial functions u0u_{0} and prove Theorem 1.3. We first prove a lemma.

∥∇V(⋅,t)∥∞=∥∇e(t−t0)​(Δ−λ​I)V(⋅,t0)+μ∫t0t∇e(t−s)​(Δ−λ​I)U(⋅,s)ds∥∞∀t≥t0.\|\nabla V(\cdot,t)\|_{\infty}=\|\nabla e^{(t-t_{0})(\Delta-\lambda I)}V(\cdot,t_{0})+\mu\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\nabla e^{(t-s)(\Delta-\lambda I)}U(\cdot,s)ds\|_{\infty}\quad\forall\,\ t\geq t_{0}.

By (2.1), (5.11), we have

∥∇e(t−t0)​(Δ−λ​I)V(⋅,t0)∥∞\displaystyle\|\nabla e^{(t-t_{0})(\Delta-\lambda I)}V(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{\infty} =∥e(t−t0)​(Δ−λ​I)∇V(⋅,t0)∥∞≤e−λ⁡(t−t0)∥∇V(⋅,t0)∥∞\displaystyle=\|e^{(t-t_{0})(\Delta-\lambda I)}\nabla V(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{\infty}\leq e^{-\lambda(t-t_{0})}\|\nabla V(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{\infty} (5.30)
≤e−λ⁡(t−t0)​2​C0b⁡(1−θ)≤2​C0b⁡(1−θ)​e−α⁡(t−t0)∀t≥t0.\displaystyle\leq e^{-\lambda(t-t_{0})}\frac{2C_{0}}{b(1-\theta)}\leq\frac{2C_{0}}{b(1-\theta)}e^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})}\quad\forall\,t\geq t_{0}. (5.31)

Furthermore, (2.2) along with the definition of TT gives us that

μ∫t0t∥∇e(t−s)​(Δ−λ​I)U(⋅,s)∥∞ds\displaystyle\mu\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\|\nabla e^{(t-s)(\Delta-\lambda I)}U(\cdot,s)\|_{\infty}ds ≤μ​C​∫t0t(t−s)−12​e−λ⁡(t−s)​‖U⁡(⋅,s)‖∞​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq\mu C\int_{t_{0}}^{t}(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\lambda(t-s)}\|U(\cdot,s)\|_{\infty}ds (5.32)
≤μ​B​C​λ−12​(∫0λ⁡(t−t0)σ−12​e−(1−αλ)​σ​𝑑σ)​e−α⁡(t−t0)\displaystyle\leq\mu BC\lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}\big(\int_{0}^{\lambda(t-t_{0})}\sigma^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-(1-\frac{\alpha}{\lambda})\sigma}d\sigma\big)e^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})} (5.33)
≤μ​B​C​λ−12​(1−αλ)−12​π​e−α⁡(t−t0)∀t∈(t0,T).\displaystyle\leq\mu BC\lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1-\frac{\alpha}{\lambda})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{\pi}e^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})}\quad\,\ \forall\,\ t\in(t_{0},T). (5.34)

Combing (5.30) and (5.32), we get that

‖∇V​(⋅,t)‖∞≤{2​C0b⁡(1−θ)+μ​B​C​λ−12​(1−αλ)−12​π}​e−α⁡(t−t0)∀t∈(t0,T).\|\nabla V(\cdot,t)\|_{\infty}\leq\big\{\frac{2C_{0}}{b(1-\theta)}+\mu BC\lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1-\frac{\alpha}{\lambda})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{\pi}\big\}e^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})}\quad\,\ \forall\,\ t\in(t_{0},T). (5.35)

By the variation of constant formula again, we have

‖U⁡(⋅,t)‖∞\displaystyle\|U(\cdot,t)\|_{\infty} ≤∥e(t−t0)​(Δ−a​I)U(⋅,t0)∥∞+χ∫t0t∥e(t−s)​(Δ−a​I)∇⋅(u(⋅,s;u0,v0)∇V(⋅,s))∥∞ds\displaystyle\leq\|e^{(t-t_{0})(\Delta-aI)}U(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{\infty}+\chi\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\|e^{(t-s)(\Delta-aI)}\nabla\cdot(u(\cdot,s;u_{0},v_{0})\nabla V(\cdot,s))\|_{\infty}ds (5.36)
+b∫t0t∥e(t−s)​(Δ−a​I)U2(⋅,s)∥∞ds∀t>t0.\displaystyle\,\,\,\,\,+b\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\|e^{(t-s)(\Delta-aI)}U^{2}(\cdot,s)\|_{\infty}ds\quad\forall\,\ t>t_{0}. (5.37)

It follows from (5.27) and (5.28) that

‖e(t−t0)​(Δ−a​I)​U​(⋅,t0)‖∞\displaystyle\|e^{(t-t_{0})(\Delta-aI)}U(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{\infty} ≤e−a⁡(t−t0)​‖U⁡(⋅,t0)‖∞≤e−a⁡(t−t0)​2​C2​θb​(1−θ)2\displaystyle\leq e^{-a(t-t_{0})}\|U(\cdot,t_{0})\|_{\infty}\leq e^{-a(t-t_{0})}\frac{2C_{2}\theta}{b(1-\theta)^{2}} (5.38)
≤e−α⁡(t−t0)​2​C2​θb​(1−θ)2≤B6​e−α⁡(t−t0)∀t>t0.\displaystyle\leq e^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})}\frac{2C_{2}\theta}{b(1-\theta)^{2}}\leq\frac{B}{6}e^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})}\quad\forall\,\ t>t_{0}. (5.39)

By Lemma 2.1, (5.2), (5.26), (5.27), (5.35), and χb=4​θN​μ\frac{\chi}{b}=\frac{4\theta}{N\mu}, we have

χ∫t0t∥e(t−s)​(Δ−a​I)∇⋅(u(⋅,s;u0,v0)∇V(⋅,s))∥∞ds\displaystyle\chi\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\|e^{(t-s)(\Delta-aI)}\nabla\cdot(u(\cdot,s;u_{0},v_{0})\nabla V(\cdot,s))\|_{\infty}ds (5.40)
≤χ​C​∫t0te−a⁡(t−s)​(t−s)−12​2​ab⁡(1−θ)​{2​C0b⁡(1−θ)+μ​B​C​λ−12​(1−αλ)−12​π}​e−α⁡(s−t0)​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq\chi C\int_{t_{0}}^{t}e^{-a(t-s)}(t-s)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\frac{2a}{b(1-\theta)}\big\{\frac{2C_{0}}{b(1-\theta)}+\mu BC\lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1-\frac{\alpha}{\lambda})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{\pi}\big\}e^{-\alpha(s-t_{0})}ds (5.41)
≤{16​θ​a​C0b​N​μ​(1−θ)2+8​θ​a​B​C​(λ−α)−12​πN⁡(1−θ)}​(a−α)−12​π​e−α⁡(t−t0)\displaystyle\leq\big\{\frac{16\theta aC_{0}}{bN\mu(1-\theta)^{2}}+\frac{8\theta aBC(\lambda-\alpha)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{\pi}}{N(1-\theta)}\big\}(a-\alpha)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{\pi}e^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})} (5.42)
≤B6​e−α⁡(t−t0)∀t∈(t0,T).\displaystyle\leq\frac{B}{6}e^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})}\quad\,\ \forall\,\ t\in(t_{0},T). (5.43)

By (5.26), (5.28), and the definition of TT, we have

b∫t0t∥e(t−s)​(Δ−a​I)U2(⋅,s))∥∞ds\displaystyle b\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\|e^{(t-s)(\Delta-aI)}U^{2}(\cdot,s))\|_{\infty}ds ≤b​∫t0te−a⁡(t−s)​‖U⁡(⋅,s)‖∞​‖U⁡(⋅,s)‖∞​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq b\int_{t_{0}}^{t}e^{-a(t-s)}\|U(\cdot,s)\|_{\infty}\|U(\cdot,s)\|_{\infty}ds (5.44)
≤b​∫t0te−a⁡(t−s)​2​C2​θb​(1−θ)2​B​e−α⁡(s−t0)​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq b\int_{t_{0}}^{t}e^{-a(t-s)}\frac{2C_{2}\theta}{b(1-\theta)^{2}}Be^{-\alpha(s-t_{0})}ds (5.45)
≤2​C2​θ(1−θ)2⋅B⋅1a−α⋅e−α⁡(t−t0)\displaystyle\leq\frac{2C_{2}\theta}{(1-\theta)^{2}}\cdot B\cdot\frac{1}{a-\alpha}\cdot e^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})} (5.46)
≤16​B​e−α⁡(t−t0)∀t∈(t0,T).\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{6}Be^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})}\quad\forall\,\ t\in(t_{0},T). (5.47)

Combing (5.38), (5.40) and (5.44), we can obtain that

‖U⁡(⋅,t)‖∞≤3⋅16​B​e−α⁡(t−t0)=B2​e−α⁡(t−t0)∀t∈(t0,T)\|U(\cdot,t)\|_{\infty}\leq 3\cdot\frac{1}{6}Be^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})}=\frac{B}{2}e^{-\alpha(t-t_{0})}\quad\forall\,\ t\in(t_{0},T)

which together with the continuity of UU implies that TT cannot be finite. This shows (5.29), and (5.25) then follows.

We now prove that there is C>0C>0 such that

‖V⁡(⋅,t)‖∞≤C​e−α​t∀t>0.\|V(\cdot,t)\|_{\infty}\leq Ce^{-\alpha t}\quad\forall\,t>0. (5.48)

By variation of constants formula associated with the second equation in (3.25), we get that

V⁡(⋅,t)=et⁡(Δ−λ​I)​(v0−μλ​ab)+μ​∫0te(t−s)​(Δ−λ​I)​U​(⋅,s)​𝑑s∀t>0.V(\cdot,t)=e^{t(\Delta-\lambda I)}\big(v_{0}-\frac{\mu}{\lambda}\frac{a}{b}\big)+\mu\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)(\Delta-\lambda I)}U(\cdot,s)ds\quad\forall\,\ t>0.

By (5.25), we have

‖V⁡(⋅,t)‖∞\displaystyle\|V(\cdot,t)\|_{\infty} ≤‖et⁡(Δ−λ​I)​(v0−μλ​ab)‖∞+μ​∫0t‖e(t−s)​(Δ−λ​I)​U​(⋅,s)‖∞​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq\|e^{t(\Delta-\lambda I)}\big(v_{0}-\frac{\mu}{\lambda}\frac{a}{b}\big)\|_{\infty}+\mu\int_{0}^{t}\|e^{(t-s)(\Delta-\lambda I)}U(\cdot,s)\|_{\infty}ds (5.49)
≤e−λ​t​‖v0−μλ​ab‖∞+C​μ​∫0te−λ⁡(t−s)​e−α​s​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq e^{-\lambda t}\|v_{0}-\frac{\mu}{\lambda}\frac{a}{b}\|_{\infty}+C\mu\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\lambda(t-s)}e^{-\alpha s}ds (5.50)
=e−λ​t​‖v0−μλ​ab‖∞+C​μλ−α​(e−α​t−e−λ​t)∀t>0.\displaystyle=e^{-\lambda t}\|v_{0}-\frac{\mu}{\lambda}\frac{a}{b}\|_{\infty}+\frac{C\mu}{\lambda-\alpha}(e^{-\alpha t}-e^{-\lambda t})\quad\forall\,\ t>0. (5.51)

(5.48) then follows, and (5.25) and (5.48) establish (1.12). ∎
